Investors Thought Moderna Was Left for Dead. Then Came a Cancer Breakthrough.
 
Plus, the secret’s out on the Catskills, and Democrats gear up for a wave of investigations into Trump and his allies
 
 
MEL MUSTO FOR WSJ
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

After years of contending with steep stock drops, cash burn and political headwinds, Moderna delivered the kind of triumph biotech startups rarely enjoy twice. Positive trial results for its personalized melanoma vaccine triggered a massive Wall Street rally, marking a dramatic second act for the company. But major regulatory and manufacturing hurdles remain. This morning, we examine how this targeted mRNA technology trains the immune system to fight cancer—and what it will take to bring it to patients.

 

Also for your weekend enjoyment: a tour of the booming real-estate market transforming the Catskills, and our auto critic Dan Neil’s dispatch from the Concours d’Lemons, where strange, unloved cars compete for “Worst in Show.”

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods after trade talks broke down late last night.

 

• President Trump is quietly making plans for another ballroom—nearly 200 miles north of the White House, in New Jersey.

 

• Trump made a personal pitch to South Carolinians on Friday, urging them to back Sen. Darline Graham in the Republican runoff primary election next week.

 

• The fall of Russia’s token antiwar party, Yabloko, has exposed President Vladimir Putin’s vulnerability.

 

• Roughly a dozen high-ranking officials were let go at Fannie Mae this week, raising concerns about more turmoil at one of the firms that back major portions of the mortgage market.

 

• Iran’s top politicians said the country needs to focus on ending the war and shoring up its economy, pushing back publicly against hardliners in the regime.

 
 
 

3. FROM THE MARKETS

 

• The Treasury Department’s announcement of a bond buyback stemmed a selloff—but not for long. We look at the wild week when Scott Bessent was schooled by the bond market.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Democrats are gearing up for a wave of investigations into Trump and his allies.

 

Needing just a handful more seats to gain control of the House in November, Democrats are preparing to use that majority to launch multifront probes into the Trump administration, while the White House is bracing for an onslaught of subpoenas. White House lawyers have briefed cabinet secretaries and top aides on how to respond. But there are early divisions within the Democratic Party over where to focus their investigative firepower and whether to impeach the president for a third time, report Natalie Andrews and Olivia Beavers. Some Democratic lawmakers worry about a voter backlash if they go too far. Others are concerned that an unwavering focus on Trump risks overshadowing Democrats’ agenda, including efforts to lower prices.

 

5.

 

AI’s need for content has put rare-book dealers in a bind.

 

For months, used-book sellers worldwide have been swapping stories of curious sales patterns. The buyers went by unusual names and ordered dozens, even hundreds of books at a time. And they didn’t haggle over prices. At first, dealers had practical concerns: How does a small shop that’s never packaged an order bigger than 20 books even ship a batch of 200? Beneath those questions lurked a growing suspicion that the orders had something to do with artificial intelligence companies’ insatiable need for new content to train their large language models. As evidence piled up that many of the mystery orders were ending up in facilities where books are sliced up, scanned and destroyed, sellers worry irreplaceable books are being “sent to the guillotine,” reports Melissa Korn.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

The Catskills were once considered a hidden gem. Now the secret’s out.

 
 
BRETT WOOD
 

Since the pandemic, New York City buyers priced out of the Hudson Valley have increasingly looked north and west to the Catskills. Their arrival has brought many multimillion-dollar renovation and new-construction projects. Now newly revamped farmhouses and sleek modern houses are appearing throughout the mountain region—and selling for once unheard-of prices.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING THIS WEEKEND

 

• Saturday: The Freedom 250 Grand Prix kicks off in Washington, D.C.

 

• Sunday: U.S. Open Fan Week begins in Flushing Meadows, headlined by a new, single-day Qualifying Wild Card Challenge.

 

• 📰 Today’s paper

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
48.9%
 

China slashing its oil imports by nearly half has been pivotal to keeping oil prices down since the start of the war in Iran. That drop, in turn, has helped curb inflation and support the global economy. How Beijing pulled off the cut and survived has been a mystery, even with Beijing’s long-term strategy of energy self-reliance. Some clues are now emerging—and we illuminate them in charts.
